[2025 summer phd math-stat — problem 3]

Part III, Problem 3 (25 pts). Let $\{(X_i, Y_i, R_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be i.i.d. with covariates $X_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, response $Y_i$, and missingness indicator $R_i \in \{0, 1\}$ ($R_i = 1$ if $Y_i$ observed). Assume (a) $Y_i \mid X_i, R_i = 1 \stackrel{d}{=} Y_i \mid X_i, R_i = 0$, and (b) $X_i \mid R_i = 1 \sim P_X$, $X_i \mid R_i = 0 \sim Q_X$ (possibly different). Target: $\beta^* = \arg\min_\beta \mathbb{E}[(Y_i - X_i^\top\beta)^2 \mid R_i = 0]$.
(i) Show $\mathbb{E}[(Y_i - X_i^\top\beta)^2 \mid R_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}[(Y_i - X_i^\top\beta)^2 \frac{f_{X|R=0}(X_i)}{f_{X|R=1}(X_i)} \mid R_i = 1]$.
(ii) Prove $\frac{f_{X|R=0}(x)}{f_{X|R=1}(x)} = \frac{P(R=0\mid x)}{P(R=1\mid x)}\cdot\frac{P(R=1)}{P(R=0)}$.
(iii) Apply (i) and (ii) to construct an estimator of $\beta^*$.

response.text:
Let  
\[
p_r=P(R=r),\qquad f_r(x)=f_{X\mid R=r}(x),\qquad r\in\{0,1\},
\]
and assume the usual overlap/positivity condition
\[
f_0(x)>0\implies f_1(x)>0,
\]
so that \(w(x):=f_0(x)/f_1(x)\) is well defined \(Q_X\)-a.e. Also assume the relevant second moments are finite.

---

## (i) Change-of-measure identity

For fixed \(\beta\), define
\[
m_\beta(x,r):=\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2\mid X=x,R=r\right].
\]
Assumption (a) says
\[
Y\mid X=x,R=1 \stackrel d= Y\mid X=x,R=0,
\]
so in particular
\[
m_\beta(x,1)=m_\beta(x,0)=:m_\beta(x).
\]

Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2\mid R=0\right]
&=\mathbb E\left[m_\beta(X)\mid R=0\right] \\
&=\int m_\beta(x) f_0(x)\,dx \\
&=\int m_\beta(x)\frac{f_0(x)}{f_1(x)} f_1(x)\,dx \\
&=\mathbb E\left[m_\beta(X)\frac{f_0(X)}{f_1(X)}\mid R=1\right] \\
&=\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(X)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(X)}\mid R=1\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus
\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2\mid R=0\right]
=
\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(X)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(X)}\mid R=1\right].
}
\]

This is simply importance weighting/covariate-shift reweighting from the observed-response covariate distribution to the missing-response covariate distribution.

---

## (ii) Bayes formula for the density ratio

By Bayes’ rule, for \(r\in\{0,1\}\),

\[
P(R=r\mid X=x)
=
\frac{f_{X\mid R=r}(x)P(R=r)}{f_X(x)}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{P(R=0\mid X=x)}{P(R=1\mid X=x)}
=
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(x)P(R=0)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(x)P(R=1)}.
\]

Rearranging gives

\[
\boxed{
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(x)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(x)}
=
\frac{P(R=0\mid X=x)}{P(R=1\mid X=x)}
\cdot
\frac{P(R=1)}{P(R=0)}.
}
\]

Equivalently, if \(\pi(x):=P(R=1\mid X=x)\), then

\[
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(x)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(x)}
=
\frac{1-\pi(x)}{\pi(x)}\cdot \frac{p_1}{p_0}.
\]

---

## (iii) Estimator of \(\beta^*\)

By parts (i) and (ii), \(\beta^*\) can be characterized as the minimizer of a weighted least-squares risk over the observed cases \(R_i=1\):

\[
\beta^*
=
\arg\min_\beta
\mathbb E\left[
(Y-X^\top\beta)^2
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(X)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(X)}
\mid R=1
\right].
\]

Using the propensity score \(\pi(x)=P(R=1\mid X=x)\),

\[
w(x)
=
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(x)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(x)}
=
\frac{1-\pi(x)}{\pi(x)}\cdot \frac{p_1}{p_0}.
\]

In practice, estimate \(\pi(x)\) from the data \(\{(X_i,R_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), for example by logistic regression or another classification method. Let \(\widehat\pi(x)\) be the fitted propensity and let

\[
\widehat p_1=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n R_i,\qquad 
\widehat p_0=1-\widehat p_1.
\]

Define the estimated weight

\[
\widehat w_i
=
\frac{1-\widehat\pi(X_i)}{\widehat\pi(X_i)}
\cdot
\frac{\widehat p_1}{\widehat p_0}.
\]

Then an estimator of \(\beta^*\) is the inverse-propensity/covariate-shift weighted least-squares estimator

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\beta
=
\arg\min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^d}
\sum_{i=1}^n
R_i\,\widehat w_i\,(Y_i-X_i^\top\beta)^2.
}
\]

The constant factor \(\widehat p_1/\widehat p_0\) does not affect the minimizer, so equivalently one may use weights

\[
\widehat a_i
=
\frac{1-\widehat\pi(X_i)}{\widehat\pi(X_i)}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\widehat\beta
=
\arg\min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^d}
\sum_{i=1}^n
R_i\,\widehat a_i\,(Y_i-X_i^\top\beta)^2.
\]

When the weighted design matrix is invertible, the closed-form estimator is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\beta
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^n R_i\,\widehat a_i\,X_iX_i^\top
\right)^{-1}
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^n R_i\,\widehat a_i\,X_iY_i
\right).
}
\]

This estimator uses only observed responses \(Y_i\) with \(R_i=1\), but reweights them so that their covariate distribution mimics the covariate distribution among the missing-response group \(R_i=0\). Under standard consistency conditions for \(\widehat\pi\), positivity, and nonsingularity of the target second-moment matrix, this weighted least-squares estimator is consistent for \(\beta^*\).
